prompt: What three things are typically needed to decipher an unknown script?
options: Patience, plenty of ink, and quiet working time
Known language, sufficient corpus, and a bilingual
Government grant, a fast computer, and luck
Carbon dating, photography, and X-ray analysis
correctAnswer: Known language, sufficient corpus, and a bilingual
explanation: Lacking even one of these makes the problem mathematically underdetermined. Egyptian hieroglyphs fell because all three were available (Greek + Demotic + hieroglyphs on the Rosetta Stone, plus living Coptic as the descendant language).

prompt: Why does corpus size matter for decipherment?
options: Larger corpora simply look more impressive on the page
Letter and n-gram patterns stabilise only with text
Bigger collections signal historical importance to readers
It is purely an arbitrary archaeological tradition
correctAnswer: Letter and n-gram patterns stabilise only with text
explanation: Frequency analysis and Markov-style structural analysis depend on having enough text for signals to rise above noise. Short corpora — like the Indus script — barely give enough data for any statistical attack to converge.

prompt: Why might an unknown script be undecipherable in principle?
options: Modern computational tools are still too primitive
Symbols may not encode speech; could be ritual marks
Specialist researchers no longer attempt translation
Modern computers cannot run the tasks fast enough
correctAnswer: Symbols may not encode speech; could be ritual marks
explanation: Decipherment assumes there's an encoded language to recover. If the symbols are non-linguistic (counting, ownership marks, religious symbols), there's nothing to decode in the linguistic sense. The Indus script may fit this category.

prompt: What did the Rosetta Stone provide for Egyptian hieroglyphs?
options: Better computational tools and palaeographic resources
A trilingual text plus Coptic, the descendant language
A famous academic decoder with full royal backing
An unprecedented level of state royal patronage support
correctAnswer: A trilingual text plus Coptic, the descendant language
explanation: Champollion combined the Greek-Egyptian alignment with knowledge of Coptic (Egyptian's descendant language) to crack both phonetic and logographic elements. The Rosetta Stone is the textbook example of how all three decipherment requirements line up.

prompt: Why do many claimed Voynich-style 'solutions' fail?
options: The original reviewers had personal academic biases
They explain a few words then stop generalising
Modern translators are reluctant to accept new ideas
Academic editors do not adequately peer-review the claims
correctAnswer: They explain a few words then stop generalising
explanation: A real decipherment must predict new words and produce coherent grammar across the corpus. Most claimed Voynich solutions don't survive that test — they cherry-pick a few suggestive matches, then can't continue.

prompt: Who used Linear A?
options: Romans of the Republic in central Italy
Minoans on Crete around 1800 to 1450 BCE
Phoenicians of the Levantine coast and trade
Old Kingdom Egyptians along the lower Nile
correctAnswer: Minoans on Crete around 1800 to 1450 BCE
explanation: Linear A was the script of the Minoan palace civilisation, surviving primarily on small clay tablets. It was succeeded by Linear B around 1450 BCE when the mainland Mycenaean Greeks took over Crete.

prompt: Why doesn't reading Linear A with Linear B's sound values produce understandable text?
options: Modern researchers have lost the values for Linear B
The two scripts encode unrelated languages
Existing copies of Linear A are simply too damaged
Linear B's sound values turned out to be all wrong
correctAnswer: The two scripts encode unrelated languages
explanation: Linear B was an adaptation of Linear A's signs to write a different language. Scholars can roughly sound out Linear A with Linear B values, but the resulting words match no known language, showing the two scripts encode different languages.

prompt: Who deciphered Linear B and when?
options: Jean-François Champollion in early 1822
Michael Ventris in 1952 with John Chadwick
Carl Sagan working at Cornell in late 1969
Alan Turing at Bletchley Park during 1942
correctAnswer: Michael Ventris in 1952 with John Chadwick
explanation: Architect-turned-amateur-classicist Michael Ventris cracked Linear B in 1952 by identifying it as an early form of Greek. He died young in a 1956 car crash. The decipherment is celebrated as the most spectacular linguistic achievement of the 20th century.

prompt: What does Linear A's failure under Linear-B rules tell us about Minoans?
options: The ancient Minoans were largely an illiterate people
Their language is an isolate, not Greek or known
The mainland Mycenaeans actually invented Linear A
We can confidently extract no information at all here
correctAnswer: Their language is an isolate, not Greek or known
explanation: If Linear A encoded Greek, Phoenician, Hittite, or any reconstructed-and-known language, the substitution would yield meaningful text. It doesn't — strong evidence the underlying language is unique and now lost.

prompt: What might allow Linear A decipherment in future?
options: A faster computer with much more memory
A bilingual text or longer monoglot corpus
Asking specialist Aegean academic experts politely
Carbon-dating each individual surviving tablet
correctAnswer: A bilingual text or longer monoglot corpus
explanation: A bilingual artefact would crack Linear A immediately. Absent that, decipherment depends on archaeology providing more text and on computational models that can constrain the underlying language's structure enough to pick a unique decoding.

prompt: Where and when did the Indus civilisation flourish?
options: Ancient Egypt around 1500 BCE along the Nile
Modern Pakistan and NW India around 2600 BCE
Mesopotamia between rivers around 3000 BCE
Eastern China during the early Shang dynasty
correctAnswer: Modern Pakistan and NW India around 2600 BCE
explanation: The Indus Valley Civilisation produced planned cities with grids, sewerage, and standardised weights. Its script is preserved on ~4,000 inscribed seals and tablets — but only in tantalisingly short inscriptions.

prompt: What is the average length of an Indus inscription?
options: About one hundred signs per inscription
About five signs per inscription on average
About fifty signs per typical inscription
About a thousand signs per inscription
correctAnswer: About five signs per inscription on average
explanation: Average ~5 signs, longest single line ~17, longest object ~26. This is far shorter than typical scripts that encode language, which is part of why some scholars argue Indus signs may not be writing in the linguistic sense.

prompt: What is the 'is it even language' debate about Indus?
options: A typographical error in the original literature
Whether signs encode speech or non-linguistic symbols
A modern academic joke without any real substance
An accusation that Indus is an archaeological hoax
correctAnswer: Whether signs encode speech or non-linguistic symbols
explanation: Steve Farmer and colleagues argued in 2004 that Indus inscriptions might be non-linguistic. Counter-arguments based on positional regularities and conditional sign frequencies (Rao et al. 2009) defend the writing hypothesis. The debate is unresolved.

prompt: What is the most-discussed candidate language for Indus?
options: Classical Sanskrit of the Vedic period
Proto-Dravidian, ancestor of South Indian
Akkadian, language of ancient Mesopotamia
Sumerian, language of southern ancient Iraq
correctAnswer: Proto-Dravidian, ancestor of South Indian
explanation: Asko Parpola's long-running work argues for Proto-Dravidian, the ancestor of modern South Indian languages like Tamil. Indo-Aryan candidates are also proposed, often with political overtones in modern India. Neither is confirmed.

prompt: Why is Indus particularly hard to decipher?
options: The surviving signs are physically illegible
Short corpus, no bilingual, uncertain status
There is no preserved corpus to analyse
Modern researchers do not actively study it
correctAnswer: Short corpus, no bilingual, uncertain status
explanation: All four obstacles compound: short corpus blocks statistics, no bilingual blocks anchoring, language uncertainty blocks targeted attack, and the ontological question about whether it's writing makes the problem ill-defined.

prompt: What is the Voynich Manuscript?
options: A nineteenth-century European literary forgery
Early-15th-century book in unknown script
A modern conceptual art piece in coded glyphs
A medieval Hebrew religious commentary text
correctAnswer: Early-15th-century book in unknown script
explanation: Carbon-dated to 1404–1438. ~240 surviving pages, hand-written, with fantastical plant drawings, women in tubs connected by piping, and zodiacal diagrams. Now Yale Beinecke MS 408.

prompt: What does statistical analysis of 'Voynichese' reveal?
options: Pure random nonsense with no underlying structure
Zipf-law frequencies and section-specific vocabulary
It is modern English written in a disguised form
The text functions as purely decorative ornament
correctAnswer: Zipf-law frequencies and section-specific vocabulary
explanation: Zipf's law alone is weak evidence (random text can produce it), but together with positional rules and section-specific vocabularies the structure is hard to fake. Either Voynichese encodes a real language, an artificial language with linguistic-quality structure, or a sophisticated cipher whose ciphertext mimics natural-language statistics — each is interesting.

prompt: Why do most claimed Voynich 'solutions' fail review?
options: The reviewers' preexisting academic biases dominate
They explain a few words but fail to generalise
Modern academic journals avoid publishing these claims
All such papers remain locked behind paywalls
correctAnswer: They explain a few words but fail to generalise
explanation: A real decipherment must predict and confirm new readings across the corpus. Most claims start with a plausible match, then the proposed system breaks down within a paragraph. Without reproducibility there's no decipherment, just a hypothesis.

prompt: What is firmly established about the Voynich Manuscript?
options: The underlying spoken language used by the author
Origin: early-15th-century European parchment
The full identity of the manuscript's actual author
The exact meaning of Voynichese on every page
correctAnswer: Origin: early-15th-century European parchment
explanation: Radiocarbon dating, ink chemistry, parchment analysis, and palaeographic comparison all point to early-15th-century Europe. Whatever Voynichese is, it isn't a modern hoax. Beyond date and origin, almost nothing is consensus knowledge.

prompt: If Voynichese shows Zipf-like word frequencies plus consistent word-structure rules and section-specific vocabularies, what remains plausible?
options: Nothing relevant to its underlying composition or origin
Real language, artificial language, or careful cipher
The text must be classical or medieval Latin disguised
The manuscript is necessarily a modern hoax of some kind
correctAnswer: Real language, artificial language, or careful cipher
explanation: Zipf-like frequencies alone can arise even from random text, but the combination with rigid word-internal rules and topic-specific vocabularies is hard to produce by chance, and a 15th-century forger would not have known to fake it. So three categories of explanation remain plausible.

prompt: Where is Rongorongo from?
options: The island of Madagascar in the Indian Ocean
Easter Island, also known as Rapa Nui
The Hawaiian island chain in the Pacific
The kingdom of Tonga in the South Pacific
correctAnswer: Easter Island, also known as Rapa Nui
explanation: Rongorongo survives on ~25 carved wooden tablets from Rapa Nui. The literate population collapsed from 19th-century disease and slave raids before any sustained contact with linguistically-trained outsiders.

prompt: How is Rongorongo read?
options: Top to bottom only, never alternating
Reverse boustrophedon, alternating lines flipped
Left to right normally with standard line breaks
In a continuous spiral inward toward the centre
correctAnswer: Reverse boustrophedon, alternating lines flipped
explanation: Reverse boustrophedon is a rare reading direction; the carver wrote one line normally, then flipped the tablet to write the next. Readers physically rotated the tablet line by line. This makes the script visually distinctive.

prompt: Why is Rongorongo unbroken if Rapa Nui language is known?
options: No serious researchers have ever tried to decipher it
Tiny corpus, no bilingual, conflicting informants
The Rapa Nui language itself is not actually known well
The original tablets were entirely destroyed long ago
correctAnswer: Tiny corpus, no bilingual, conflicting informants
explanation: Even with the language known, decipherment needs a way to anchor specific signs to specific sounds. The 19th-century informants who claimed to read tablets gave inconsistent accounts. Modern statistical attacks on the small corpus have not converged.

prompt: What is Proto-Elamite?
options: A modern artificially-constructed language for academic use
Undeciphered ~3100–2900 BCE script from ancient Iran
A 20th-century cipher used in mid-century cryptography
A Mesopotamian dialect of Akkadian once widely spoken
correctAnswer: Undeciphered ~3100–2900 BCE script from ancient Iran
explanation: Proto-Elamite is one of the earliest writing systems known. Its underlying language is hypothesised to be ancestral to Elamite (which we can read), but confirming that requires breaking Proto-Elamite — a circular dependency.

prompt: What general lesson do undeciphered scripts illustrate?
options: History as a discipline is fundamentally uninteresting
Information lost from context can be permanently lost
All ancient scripts are eventually deciphered with patience
Sufficient computational power will eventually solve everything
correctAnswer: Information lost from context can be permanently lost
explanation: A short corpus in an unknown language is mathematically underdetermined regardless of how much compute you throw at it. The structural information needed to decipher must come from outside — a bilingual text, a known descendant language, or sufficient corpus. None of these can be conjured.
